extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics educators, mathematics-education researchers, and instructors using Python to teach combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and explaining Python-based activities (loops and conditionals) to help undergraduate students reason about canonical combinatorial problem types and connect computational outputs to combinatorial formulas. Includes annotated code, pedagogical choices, and mapping between program constructs and counting interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conditional statements to represent combinatorial problem types
rubrics_metrics.description: Four straightforward program conditional statements seemed to reinforce important conceptual understandings of four canonical combinatorial problem types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map specific conditional tests to the combinatorial constraint you want students to attend to. Examples in the paper: 'if j != i' to enforce no-repetition pairs; using '>=' (greater than or equal to) corresponds to counting non-decreasing sequences (selection with repetition). The conditional structure makes explicit which outcomes are included/excluded and thus highlights the problem type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit the multiplication principle
rubrics_metrics.description: This reflects the multiplication principle, which is a guiding principle that describes when it is appropriate to multiply in counting problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use code and discussion to surface when independent choices multiply to give total outcomes; connect program iteration counts (e.g., nested loops producing product counts) to the multiplication principle as a pedagogical target (references: Tucker 2002; Lockwood et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encode outcomes using 'xs' and 'bars' for selection with repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode outcomes as strings of xs and bars so counting selection-with-repetition reduces to choosing positions (leading to the formula C(n + r - 1, r)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: hot-dog problem with 6 types and 3 selections encoded as 3 xs and 5 bars (strings of length 8); counting choices of positions for xs yields C(8,3). Use this encoding to link program-generated outcome lists to the closed-form combinatorial formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nested for loops to enumerate outcome spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The command 'for i in Numbers:' and nested 'for j in Numbers:' will iterate through every ordered pair (i,j) producing the full sample space in code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain loop nesting and iteration counts to students: e.g., two nested loops over a length-5 list produce 25 iterations (ordered pairs). Use nested loops to generate ordered outcomes; vary nesting depth to generate tuples of different lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place conditional checks inside loops to enforce combinatorial constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: For each value of i and j the program will follow the command 'if j != i:'—as long as the condition is met the program carries out the nested instructions to print the pair and increment the counter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how conditionals inside loops filter the enumerated sample space to produce only desired outcomes (e.g., no-repetition, j > i to enforce ordering). Emphasize that the conditional determines whether the counter increments or whether an outcome is printed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a counter variable to track the number of generated outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and initialize 'Counter = 0' and increment the counter each time a new outcome is produced; print the counter at the end to report total arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates programmatic tallying and links printed counter value to combinatorial totals; illustrate with line numbers and exact places where Counter is updated (e.g., increment in the body of an if-statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate code and explain Python syntax/semantics for novices
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide annotated code (with labeled line numbers) and explanations of Python basics such as indentation determining nesting and the meaning of '=' as assignment rather than mathematical equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting code to students unfamiliar with programming, label lines and explain indentation-based nesting, the semantics of assignment (Counter = Counter + 1 defines a new value), and how print statements work. This scaffolding helps students focus on combinatorial ideas rather than syntax confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect computational and mathematical representations to support learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Both computational and noncomputational ideas and representations contribute to the milieu in which students work; a computational setting may facilitate mathematical learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use program outputs, encodings, and visual listings of outcomes alongside traditional combinatorial explanations to help students reconcile differing answers and develop conceptual interpretations (e.g., sets of outcomes, multiplication principle). Computational models can be used both to understand and to construct mathematical ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose problem types and scope intentionally based on instructional goals and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The study did not include selection-with-repetition problems in some parts due to scope limits; students' prior exposure (e.g., factorial interpretations) affects whether particular combinatorial interpretations are assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing activities or studies, select which canonical problem types to include based on time, learning goals, and students' prior knowledge. Note that exclusion of certain types (e.g., selection with repetition) may be necessary for manageable scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tasks to tooling and display limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: This change was made to reduce the number of outcomes, as PyCharm did not easily display all the outcomes in the original problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instructional design: reduce problem size or otherwise adapt output representation when IDEs or class settings cannot display large outcome lists. Make these adaptations explicit to students and explain how the smaller case generalizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight combinatorial interpretations of factorials and permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe that n! is the product of positive integers from 1 to n, but exposure to factorials in calculus does not imply students have the combinatorial interpretation of n! as the number of arrangements of n distinct elements; P(n,r) = n!/(n-r)! counts r-permutations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly teach the combinatorial meaning of factorial and permutations and relate special cases (e.g., P(n,n) = n!) to arrangements. Use programming enumerations to illustrate these formulas concretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inequality-based constraints that subsume redundant conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Including j > i also subsumes the case in which j might be equal to i. Thus, we do not need to include both j != i and j > i, as the j > i includes these cases. Including additional constraints like k > i or j != i would not be incorrect, but they are not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing conditionals, choose minimal constraints that capture the intended outcome set to avoid redundancy and make the mapping between code and combinatorial concept clearer. Discuss how particular inequalities include or exclude equality cases and how that affects counts.
